passage:
Tuesday, 11.40 pm, finally home.
Okay. Deep breath. I'm still shaking a little. Coming back from the late shift, a police jeep flashed its light at me near the flyover and an officer waved me to the side. My heart was BANGING. My first thought was to walk faster. I didn't. I kept both hands where they could see them, said "Good evening," and held out my ID before they asked. "May I know why I've been stopped?" It was a routine check. The officer looked at my ID, asked where I was going, and let me go in two minutes. I had Anjali on a call the whole time with the phone in my pocket, and she stayed quiet and listened. She says I did everything right. 🙂 I'm going to sleep now.

qa.q: Where was the diary writer stopped by the police jeep?
What was the diary writer feeling when the officer waved to the side?
qa.a: Fear, since the heart was banging and the first urge was to walk faster.

qa.q: What helped the stop go smoothly?
qa.a: Keeping both hands visible, being polite, showing ID, asking calmly why the stop happened and having Anjali on the call.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt listening on the phone during the stop?
qa.a: Probably anxious and helpless, but she stayed quiet so the writer could focus, and afterwards she was proud.

grounding: Stopped at night by police, the protagonist is afraid but stays calm, keeps hands visible, is polite, shows ID, asks the reason and has someone on the phone.

passage:
Dear Yusuf,

You asked why I sounded strange on the phone on Friday. Here's what happened. I was riding back from the library at 11:30, and a police jeep flashed its lights and waved me over near the flyover. My heart was pounding so hard I could hear it.

I remembered what Ammi always says. I switched off the scooter, took off my helmet slowly, and kept both hands on the handlebar. I said, "Good evening, sir. May I know why I've been stopped?" He said there'd been a chain-snatching nearby. I showed my college ID and licence. I asked, politely, if I could call my brother. That was when I called you.

They let me go after ten minutes. My hands shook all the way home. I didn't argue, I didn't run, and I'm glad. Next time, I'm taking the main road.

Trisha

qa.q: At what time was Trisha riding back from the library?
What was Trisha feeling when the jeep flashed its lights?
qa.a: Trisha felt frightened, with a pounding heart, and was still shaking on the ride home.

qa.q: Which of Trisha's choices helped keep the stop calm?
qa.a: Keeping hands visible, speaking politely, asking the reason, showing ID and asking to call family helped, instead of arguing or running.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have felt getting that phone call?
qa.a: Yusuf probably felt worried but relieved to be called, since it meant someone knew where Trisha was.

grounding: The letter shows a young person stopped by police at night who stays calm, keeps hands visible, asks the reason, carries ID and calls someone.

passage:
Gautam, you asked what my scariest night in Bengaluru was. It's Elizabeth, remember, the one who never gets scared? Well. Last December I was driving back from a friend's birthday at midnight, and there was a police barricade. The officer shone a torch in my face and said, "Get out."

My knees went weak. Every part of me wanted to argue, it's my car, I've done nothing. Instead I kept my hands on the steering wheel and said, "Of course. Can you tell me why, officer?" He said it was a drunk-driving check. I blew into the machine. I had my licence and the car papers in the glove box, and I told him before reaching for them.

While he checked, I called my dad and put him on speaker. The officer returned my licence and said, "Okay, go."

I drove home at twenty kilometres an hour, still shaking.

qa.q: What kind of check was the police barricade doing?
What was Elizabeth feeling when the officer said "Get out"?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt scared, with weak knees, and also wanted to argue that nothing wrong had been done.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth stay safe during the stop?
qa.a: Elizabeth kept hands visible, asked the reason politely, said so before reaching for the papers, and called Dad on speaker.

qa.q: How might the officer see a driver who stays calm and polite?
qa.a: The officer is likely to feel less tense and finish the check quickly, as happened when he returned the licence.

grounding: The monologue shows a young person stopped by police at night who stays calm, keeps hands visible, asks the reason and calls family.
